articles.title: AI Agent or Workflow Automation? A Decision Test for Swiss SMEs
articles.excerpt: AI Agent or Workflow Automation? A Decision Test for Swiss SMEs Short answer: choose the least autonomous system that can meet the real task. Use deterministic automation when the inputs, rules, and a…
articles.body: AI Agent or Workflow Automation? A Decision Test for Swiss SMEs Short answer: choose the least autonomous system that can meet the real task. Use deterministic automation when the inputs, rules, and acceptable output are stable; use an AI-assisted workflow when language or classification is uncertain but a person can review the result; consider an agent only when the task genuinely needs flexible multi-step decisions, the available actions are bounded, errors are reversible, and a measured pilot shows better outcomes than the simpler alternatives. The useful first purchase is often not a model. It is a one-page process description, a small set of real examples, and an acceptance test.

articles.title: Knovum 0.0.2: Building an Open-Source Local-First AI Canvas with Tauri 2, Vue 3, and Rust
articles.excerpt: Like many developers and researchers, I've spent the past two years experimenting with local LLMs (via Ollama) and local RAG. But existing desktop frontends repeatedly hit two frustrating walls: The 1…
articles.body: Like many developers and researchers, I've spent the past two years experimenting with local LLMs (via Ollama) and local RAG. But existing desktop frontends repeatedly hit two frustrating walls: The 1D Chat Trap : Linear chat streams work well for simple Q&A, but break down during deep research synthesis. Earlier reasoning turns scroll off the top, and you cannot visually compare multiple document excerpts side-by-side. The Electron Memory Tax : Most desktop AI wrappers idle at 700MB–1GB RAM before you even load model weights into VRAM. To solve this, we built Knovum — an open-source, local-first desktop AI knowledge workspace built on an infinite 2D canvas with Tauri 2, Rust, and Vue 3.

articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady. My downloads folder is a list of decisions I keep postponing. Slow and Steady is a local AI assistant that…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady . What I Built My downloads folder is a list of decisions I keep postponing. Slow and Steady is a local AI assistant that suggests where files belong, so I can review a list instead of sorting everything manually. It uses Qwen2.5 1.5B through Ollama to classify filenames into categories such as finance, work, personal and reading. An invoice and meeting notes can both be text files while belonging in different folders. The workflow is: plan → review → approve → tidy → undo . Planning never moves existing files. Applying displays the proposed paths and requires approval tied to that exact plan. Uncertain files stay put.

articles.title: ChatGPT meeting notes prompt: 4 parts that stop invented details
articles.excerpt: Pasting rough meeting notes into ChatGPT with "summarize this" usually gets you something that reads well and is hard to use. Action items are buried in paragraphs, owners and deadlines go missing, an…
articles.body: Pasting rough meeting notes into ChatGPT with "summarize this" usually gets you something that reads well and is hard to use. Action items are buried in paragraphs, owners and deadlines go missing, and occasionally the model fills a gap with something nobody said. The fix is to tell it what you want in four parts. TL;DR: state the task, the output format, the rules about what it may not add, and the length. The four parts Task: say what you want made. "Turn the meeting notes below into meeting minutes." Saying "minutes" instead of "summary" already changes the result, because minutes have a known structure. Format: name the sections. "Use three sections in this order: Decisions / Action items (owner, due date) / Next meeting.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.
